clue.text: Copper worker with material left

indicators.note: the material is left, meaning it sits on the left side, ahead of the worker in the finished word

parts.note: serge is a hard-wearing twilled fabric
the worker ant is the crossword's stock worker

explanation.surface: A worker in the copper trade goes about with some cloth left over.
explanation.walkthrough: Copper here is the slang word for a police officer, not the metal; the worker is an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A copper is a police officer, and a sergeant is one particular rank of police officer, so this is an example.

clue.text: Refuse explorer, namely Hawkeye?

parts.note: sc is scilicet, Latin for namely
Hawkeye is one of Marvel's Avengers superheroes

explanation.surface: Is the archer Hawkeye some sort of explorer who refused?
explanation.walkthrough: Refuse is the noun, rubbish, not the verb to decline.
explanation.definitionFit: A scavenger searches through rubbish for anything usable, so someone who explores refuse.

clue.text: Go off eating large perch

indicators.note: a thing eating another takes it inside itself

parts.note: food that goes off rots
OS is outsize, a clothing size label

explanation.surface: A big perch, the fish, goes bad after being eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: Perch suggests the fish, given eating; it is the bird's resting place.
explanation.definitionFit: A roost is a place where birds settle to rest, the same thing as a perch.

clue.text: Get ready in area of monastery that's cutting edge

indicators.note: cutting the edge means trimming off the outer end letter of the word before

parts.note: en is French for in
a cloister garden is an area of a monastery

explanation.surface: Monks prepare for something new in their cloister.
explanation.walkthrough: In is French here, and the end letter of the monastery's area is trimmed. 'Cutting edge' also hints at a blade, suiting the fencing call.
explanation.definitionFit: En garde is the fencer's call telling an opponent to take guard, so a command to prepare for combat.

clue.text: An elevated feature of Harry Potter's sport

indicators.note: in a down entry something elevated is lifted up, so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
Harry Potter's lightning-bolt scar on his forehead

explanation.surface: Something high up in the wizarding game Harry Potter plays, quidditch.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Potter's sport suggests quidditch, but the possessive belongs to the scar.
explanation.definitionFit: NASCAR is the American stock-car racing series, a popular motor sport in the United States.

clue.text: Protective clothing taken into a shower

indicators.note: something taken into something else ends up held inside it

parts.note: a, as in 'ten pounds a head', means per
PPE is personal protective equipment

explanation.surface: Someone takes their safety gear into the shower with them.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the verb: to shower someone with things is to pepper them.
explanation.definitionFit: To pepper someone with questions or pellets is to shower them, raining many small items on them.

clue.text: Shape … is missing base

indicators.note: in a down entry the base is the bottom letter, and missing it means it is dropped

parts.note: the three dots are an ellipsis; ellipses is the plural

explanation.surface: A shape trails off into dots, as if something is missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The three dots stand for the punctuation mark's name in its plural form, then lose their last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An ellipse is a regular oval curve, a geometric figure and therefore a kind of shape.

clue.text: Turn libertine into Prime Minister with energy

indicators.note: one thing put into another goes inside it

parts.note: William Pitt, father or son, was British Prime Minister
a roué is a debauched man, a libertine
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: An energetic PM turns into a womaniser.
explanation.walkthrough: Turn libertine into Prime Minister reads like a transformation; turn is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A pirouette is a spin on one foot in ballet, a complete turn of the body.

clue.text: English setter's team at work, reflecting need to breed, perhaps

indicators.note: a reflection shows everything back to front, so the letters run in reverse order

parts.note: standard abbreviation for English
the setter refers to themself as me, so the setter's is my
HR, human resources, is the personnel team at a workplace

explanation.surface: An English setter dog is put to stud, as a working team mulls the need for it to breed.
explanation.walkthrough: English setter looks like the dog breed, matching breed; it is the compiler. The definition is an example: need and breed sound alike at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Need and breed end in the same sound, so the pair is an example of words that chime together.

clue.text: American pine throughout

parts.note: standard abbreviation for American
to pine for something is to long for it

explanation.surface: A pine tree from America is found all over.
explanation.walkthrough: Pine looks like the tree but is the verb meaning to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: As in 'all along', the word can mean for the whole time or the entire way, which is throughout.

clue.text: Barmy Army is ill in the same way

indicators.note: barmy means crazy, so the following letters go mad and come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: England's travelling cricket fans, the Barmy Army, are all sick with the same bug.
explanation.walkthrough: The Barmy Army is the famous band of England cricket supporters, so the first two words look like one name; Barmy alone is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Similarly is the adverb for doing something likewise, matching another case closely.

clue.text: Guide people to river

parts.note: men as people
taken as written
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Lead people down to the river.
explanation.definitionFit: A mentor is a trusted adviser who counsels a less experienced person, so a guide.

clue.text: Come into money without a cheer

parts.note: to come into a room is to enter it

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so the money goes around the next item

parts.note: tin is old slang for money
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone inherits a fortune but gets no applause for it.
explanation.walkthrough: Without here means outside, not lacking: the money sits around the A.
explanation.definitionFit: To entertain guests is to amuse and gladden them, which is to cheer them up.

clue.text: Suspect professor with European crest

parts.note: Professor Plum is one of the suspects in the board game Cluedo
standard abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A dodgy academic sports a European coat of arms.
explanation.walkthrough: Cluedo (Clue in North America) is the murder-mystery board game whose suspects include Professor Plum.
explanation.definitionFit: A plume of feathers worn on a helmet or bird's head is a crest, a decorative tuft on top.

clue.text: Toy gun filled with dead round, say

indicators.note: a thing filled with something holds it inside

parts.note: gat is old gangster slang for a pistol
D is the abbreviation for dead

indicators.note: turned round, the abbreviation for 'for example' runs the other way

parts.note: say means for example, abbreviated eg

explanation.surface: A toy pistol is loaded with a blank, as it were.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead round' reads like a spent cartridge, but round is the turning signal for the abbreviation of say.
explanation.definitionFit: A gadget is a clever little device, and a toy is a plaything or trinket of that kind.

clue.text: WI member to finish skirt before May

parts.note: to do something in the sense of finishing it off, as in 'that's done'
a miniskirt
may as in being allowed: you may, you can

explanation.surface: A Women's Institute member must finish her skirt before the month of May.
explanation.walkthrough: WI suggests the Women's Institute, a British women's club; here it is the West Indies, and May is the verb, not the month.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dominican is a citizen of Dominica, an island nation in the West Indies, or WI.

clue.text: Head of dinosaur — it comes off Barney

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of dinosaur

indicators.note: off means gone bad or out of order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Barney, the purple children's-TV dinosaur, has his head come off.
explanation.walkthrough: Barney looks like the TV dinosaur, but a barney is British slang for a noisy row; a domestic is likewise a household quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang both words name a heated argument, especially a row between partners at home.

clue.text: Infinite, unlike Dracula?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: too many to be numbered
second meaning, read whimsically: Dracula is a Count, so someone unlike him is without a Count

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful split of the word into a noble title plus a suffix meaning without.
explanation.definitionFit: Countless means beyond counting, too numerous to number, which is effectively infinite; and Dracula holds the title Count.

clue.text: Murder victim's hitman filmed adopting new name

indicators.note: adopting something takes it in, so the following letters go inside

parts.note: Léon, the 1994 Luc Besson film about a hitman
standard abbreviation for new
standard abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A film shows the hitman who killed someone taking on a fresh alias.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', joining definition and wordplay; John Lennon was shot dead in New York in 1980.
explanation.definitionFit: John Lennon of the Beatles was shot dead outside his home in 1980, so he was a murder victim.

clue.text: Politician going on about honour

indicators.note: the politician goes on after, attached to the end of the next item

parts.note: re means about or concerning
a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician bangs on about honour.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'going on' as placed after: the word for about comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: To remember the fallen is to honour and commemorate them, keeping them in mind with respect.

clue.text: Mixed metaphor, initially longer, getting edited

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the word it follows

parts.note: the first letter of metaphor

indicators.note: edited text is reworked, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An editor makes a mixed metaphor longer at first.
explanation.walkthrough: Mixed metaphor reads as one phrase; mixed alone is the definition, as an adjective for a dog of mixed breed.
explanation.definitionFit: A mongrel is a dog of mixed or unknown breeding, so the word describes something of mixed origin.

clue.text: Bus largely covering waste department

indicators.note: one thing covering another wraps around it
largely means most but not all, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: taken as written
urea is the waste compound excreted in urine

explanation.surface: Buses carry rubbish for the council's waste department.
explanation.walkthrough: Waste is not the verb or dustbin rubbish but a bodily waste product.
explanation.definitionFit: A bureau is a government office or agency, such as the Federal Bureau of Investigation, so a department.

clue.text: Shylock, say, claiming power for Claudius?

indicators.note: claiming something takes hold of it, so the next letter is held inside

parts.note: Shylock is the moneylender in The Merchant of Venice
P is the symbol for power

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Shylock claims power on Claudius's behalf.
explanation.walkthrough: Both names are Shakespearean: Claudius murders his brother in Hamlet and takes the throne.
explanation.definitionFit: Claudius seized the Danish crown by murdering the king, making him an example of one who wrongly takes power.

clue.text: Measure of frenzy means this accelerates

indicators.note: a measure of something is a portion of it, so a run of letters is taken from inside

parts.note: letters lifted from across the two words

explanation.surface: A frenzied mood makes things speed up.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: an enzyme is a biological catalyst.
explanation.definitionFit: Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions in living cells, acting as catalysts.

clue.text: Rule about French turn-down?

parts.note: ca is circa, Latin for about
non is French for no, a refusal

explanation.surface: A rule concerning a French bed-making ritual of turning down the sheets.
explanation.walkthrough: Turn-down suggests hotel bed service; here it is a refusal.
explanation.definitionFit: A canon is a general law or principle, as in church canon law, so a rule.

clue.text: Beast from legendary place ignored by books

indicators.note: something ignored is left out, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: King Arthur's legendary court
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A mythical creature from a fabled land that the books overlook.
explanation.definitionFit: A camel is a large humped animal, so a beast in the sense of a large four-legged creature.

clue.text: Almost any food stocked by web site in Massachusetts

indicators.note: goods stocked by a shop are held within it

parts.note: a net is a web, and the Net is the web

indicators.note: almost all of a word means it is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: taken as written
tuck is British school slang for food, especially snacks

explanation.surface: Nearly every food is sold on some website based in Massachusetts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Web site' looks like one word; web gives the letters and site begins the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Nantucket is an island and town off Cape Cod, a well-known place in the state of Massachusetts.

clue.text: King not as clear without queen's throne

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king

indicators.note: without means lacking, so those letters are removed

parts.note: hazier means less clear
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A king's throne is less obvious without the queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Khazi is British slang for a lavatory, and throne is the jokey name for a toilet seat.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are humorous slang for a toilet; throne jokes that one sits there like a monarch.

clue.text: Lord's people aren't dancing with unknown knight

parts.note: the Marylebone Cricket Club, which owns Lord's cricket ground in London

indicators.note: letters that are dancing move about and land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
y is an unknown quantity in algebra

explanation.surface: Members of the House of Lords refuse to dance alongside an obscure knight.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the London cricket ground, not the peerage; Sir Paul McCartney is the knighted Beatle.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul McCartney was knighted in 1997 and is called Sir Paul, so he is an example of a knight.

clue.text: Stage audience's worry

indicators.note: an audience hears the word rather than reading it

parts.note: to faze someone is to disconcert or worry them

explanation.surface: A stage performer's fear of the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: Stage looks like the theatre, matching audience, but it means a step in a process.
explanation.definitionFit: A phase is a distinct period or step in a process of development, which is a stage.

clue.text: Abandoned half of capital city

indicators.note: only half of the word is kept, so the second three letters are dropped

parts.note: the capital of the UK
Ely is a small cathedral city in Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: Half of a capital city lies deserted.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital and city look like one phrase; they are two places, London and Ely.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lonely feels isolated and forsaken, as if abandoned by friends and company.

clue.text: Sailors catch ropes

parts.note: to catch what someone says is to hear it
ropes as a verb: to bind or fasten

explanation.surface: Seamen grab the rigging.
explanation.walkthrough: Catch and ropes both look like sailors' actions on deck, but catch means hear.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearties is an old jocular term for seamen, as in 'me hearties', so sailors or shipmates.
